source.title: Catapults in SGD: spikes in the training loss and their impact on generalization through feature learning
source.authors: Libin Zhu; Chaoyue Liu; Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan; Mikhail Belkin

record.tranche_reason: The study varies SGD batch size and reports test performance, catapult counts, and AGOP alignment; this conceptually tests the batch-size/generalization relationship in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper also compares optimizers in Fig. 11, but the supplied text gives only plots and a qualitative statement that test performance correlates with AGOP alignment; no optimizer ranking is stated. Those figure-only comparisons are not extracted as separately attributable numeric rows. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: Figure 11 directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD and momentum SGD on held-out image-classification performance, bearing on V4. The batch-size experiments do not test V5's fixed-epoch condition: training stops at loss below 10^-3, and performance is selected using validation results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors attribute SGD loss spikes to catapults in the tangent kernel's top eigenspace and argue that smaller batches improve generalization through more catapults and greater AGOP alignment. They report negligible batch-size effects at sufficiently small learning rates. The experiments establish associations consistent with this explanation, rather than isolating AGOP alignment as a causal mediator.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines catapult dynamics, AGOP alignment, and batch-size effects rather than random-label memorization, interpolation-threshold width sweeps, or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and learning rate: smaller batches are associated with improved test performance at the larger learning rate, while batch size has little effect at the smaller learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: At learning rate ηcrit/2, rank-2 regression test loss decreases from 0.74 with full-batch GD to 0.42 with batch size 5; smaller batches also improve image-classification performance in Figure 9. Training ends at a loss threshold, rather than an equal epoch budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With a common learning rate and loss-threshold stopping, smaller batches can improve held-out performance alongside increased catapult counts and AGOP alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: At ηcrit/40, the authors report little batch-size dependence across synthetic regression, SVHN, and CelebA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the study's stopping and validation protocol, batch-size effects depend on learning rate and become negligible at sufficiently small learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: AGOP alignment correlates with held-out performance across catapult counts and optimizers; this measures feature alignment rather than magnitude-aware weight sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment between model and target AGOP predicts held-out performance in the tested tasks.

record.problems: Generalization evidence is primarily plotted; Table 1 gives a small synthetic-task batch-size comparison. Results are averaged over 3 independent runs for Fig. 9, but Table 1 does not state uncertainty. For real-world tasks, the true AGOP is estimated using a state-of-the-art model substitute.
record.rows_left_out: Optimizer comparisons in Fig. 11 are shown only as plots; the text gives no individual optimizer outcomes, so they are not extracted as rows. Other batch-size settings and datasets in Figs. 9, 29, and 32 are figure-only and were omitted; Table 1 provides explicit test-loss values for the synthetic rank-2 batch-size comparison.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same training recipe.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks; systematic learning-rate and schedule tuning; broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers. Individual optimizer outcomes in Figure 11 cannot be reliably recovered from the supplied text rendering.
Batch-size penalties with epochs held fixed, and their removal through longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 11 tests V4 using selected learning rates that the authors explicitly did not fine-tune for best test performance. Its individual held-out outcomes are unreadable in the supplied text, so no directional verdict is justified. Those comparisons and the additional batch-size plots are already declared in rows_left_out and therefore are not listed as missing. No reported experiment tests V5's defining fixed-epoch condition.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep across the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance; Fig. 11 plots optimizer comparisons but the text does not state their individual outcomes.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets, language models, and the specific recipe adaptations named in the version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training-test gap.

rows.subject: 2-layer FCN
rows.stage_stated: trained until training loss was less than 10−3
rows.operation_detail: SGD batch-size comparison with a constant learning rate; reports test loss, AGOP alignment, and catapult count.
rows.note: Table 1 reports the aggregate value for this batch size; the accompanying text says test loss decreases as batch size decreases.
rows.check: Synthetic regression trained to a loss threshold does not measure V5's fixed-epoch image-classification or language-model effect. The reported loss 0.74 is correct; batch 2000 is full-batch GD. Batch 5, with loss 0.42, supplies the relevant comparison.
